The figure that now stood by its bows was tall and swart, with one white tooth evilly protruding from its steel-like lips. A rumpled Chinese jacket of black cotton funereally invested him, with wide black trowsers of the same dark stuff. But strangely crowning this ebonness was a glistening white plaited turban, the living hair braided and coiled round and round upon his head. Less swart in aspect, the companions of this figure were of that vivid, tiger-yellow complexion peculiar to some of the aboriginal natives of the Manillas;—a race notorious for a certain diabolism of subtilty, and by some honest white mariners supposed to be the paid spies and secret confidential agents on the water of the devil, their lord, whose counting-room they suppose to be elsewhere.
While yet the wondering ship’s company were gazing upon these strangers, Ahab cried out to the white-turbaned old man at their head, “All ready there, Fedallah?”
“Ready,” was the half-hissed reply.
“Lower away then; d’ye hear?” shouting across the deck. “Lower away there, I say.”

Such was the thunder of his voice, that spite of their amazement the men sprang over the rail; the sheaves whirled round in the blocks; with a wallow, the three boats dropped into the sea; while, with a dexterous, off-handed daring, unknown in any other vocation, the sailors, goat-like, leaped down the rolling ship’s side into the tossed boats below.

Hardly had they pulled out from under the ship’s lee, when a fourth keel, coming from the windward side, pulled round under the stern, and showed the five strangers rowing Ahab, who, standing erect in the stern, loudly hailed Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask, to spread themselves widely, so as to cover a large expanse of water. “Spread yourselves,” cried Ahab; “give way, all four boats. Thou, Flask, pull out more to leeward!”
“Aye, aye, sir,” cheerily cried little King-Post, sweeping round his great steering oar. “Lay back!” addressing his crew. “There!—there!—there again! There she blows right ahead, boys!—lay back!”
“Never heed yonder yellow boys, Archy.”
“Oh, I don’t mind ’em, sir,” said Archy; “I knew it all before now. Didn’t I hear ’em in the hold? And didn’t I tell Cabaco here of it? What say ye, Cabaco? They are stowaways, Mr. Flask.”

What is it you stare at? Those chaps in yonder boat? Tut! They are only five more hands come to help us—never mind from where—the more the merrier. Pull, then, do pull; never mind the brimstone—devils are good fellows enough. So, so; there you are now; that’s the stroke for a thousand pounds; that’s the stroke to sweep the stakes! “Every man look out along his oars!” cried Starbuck. “Thou, Queequeg, stand up!”

Nimbly springing up on the triangular raised box in the bow, the savage stood erect there, and with intensely eager eyes gazed off towards the spot where the chase had last been descried. Likewise upon the extreme stern of the boat where it was also triangularly platformed level with the gunwale, Starbuck himself was seen coolly and adroitly balancing himself to the jerking tossings of his chip of a craft, and silently eyeing the vast blue eye of the sea.

It is used for catching turns with the whale line. Its top is not more spacious than the palm of a man’s hand, and standing upon such a base as that, Flask seemed perched at the mast-head of some ship which had sunk to all but her trucks. But little King-Post was small and short, and at the same time little King-Post was full of a large and tall ambition, so that this loggerhead stand-point of his did by no means satisfy King-Post.
“I can’t see three seas off; tip us up an oar there, and let me on to that.”
Upon this, Daggoo, with either hand upon the gunwale to steady his way, swiftly slid aft, and then erecting himself volunteered his lofty shoulders for a pedestal.
“Good a mast-head as any, sir. Will you mount?”
“That I will, and thank ye very much, my fine fellow; only I wish you fifty feet taller.”

And here was Flask now standing, Daggoo with one lifted arm furnishing him with a breastband to lean against and steady himself by.

At any time it is a strange sight to the tyro to see with what wondrous habitude of unconscious skill the whaleman will maintain an erect posture in his boat, even when pitched about by the most riotously perverse and cross-running seas. Still more strange to see him giddily perched upon the loggerhead itself, under such circumstances. But the sight of little Flask mounted upon gigantic Daggoo was yet more curious; for sustaining himself with a cool, indifferent, easy, unthought of, barbaric majesty, the noble negro to every roll of the sea harmoniously rolled his fine form. On his broad back, flaxen-haired Flask seemed a snow-flake. The bearer looked nobler than the rider. Though truly vivacious, tumultuous, ostentatious little Flask would now and then stamp with impatience; but not one added heave did he thereby give to the negro’s lordly chest. So have I seen Passion and Vanity stamping the living magnanimous earth, but the earth did not alter her tides and her seasons for that.

Meanwhile Stubb, the third mate, betrayed no such far-gazing solicitudes. The whales might have made one of their regular soundings, not a temporary dive from mere fright; and if that were the case, Stubb, as his wont in such cases, it seems, was resolved to solace the languishing interval with his pipe. He withdrew it from his hatband, where he always wore it aslant like a feather. He loaded it, and rammed home the loading with his thumb-end; but hardly had he ignited his match across the rough sandpaper of his hand, when Tashtego, his harpooneer, whose eyes had been setting to windward like two fixed stars, suddenly dropped like light from his erect attitude to his seat, crying out in a quick phrensy of hurry, “Down, down all, and give way!—there they are!”

To a landsman, no whale, nor any sign of a herring, would have been visible at that moment; nothing but a troubled bit of greenish white water, and thin scattered puffs of vapor hovering over it, and suffusingly blowing off to leeward, like the confused scud from white rolling billows. The air around suddenly vibrated and tingled, as it were, like the air over intensely heated plates of iron. Beneath this atmospheric waving and curling, and partially beneath a thin layer of water, also, the whales were swimming. Seen in advance of all the other indications, the puffs of vapor they spouted, seemed their forerunning couriers and detached flying outriders.

All four boats were now in keen pursuit of that one spot of troubled water and air. But it bade fair to outstrip them; it flew on and on, as a mass of interblending bubbles borne down a rapid stream from the hills.

“Pull, pull, my good boys,” said Starbuck, in the lowest possible but intensest concentrated whisper to his men; while the sharp fixed glance from his eyes darted straight ahead of the bow, almost seemed as two visible needles in two unerring binnacle compasses. He did not say much to his crew, though, nor did his crew say anything to him. Only the silence of the boat was at intervals startlingly pierced by one of his peculiar whispers, now harsh with command, now soft with entreaty.

How different the loud little King-Post. “Sing out and say something, my hearties. Roar and pull, my thunderbolts! Beach me, beach me on their black backs, boys; only do that for me, and I’ll sign over to you my Martha’s Vineyard plantation, boys; including wife and children, boys. Lay me on—lay me on! O Lord, Lord! but I shall go stark, staring mad! See! see that white water!” And so shouting, he pulled his hat from his head, and stamped up and down on it; then picking it up, flirted it far off upon the sea; and finally fell to rearing and plunging in the boat’s stern like a crazed colt from the prairie.

“Look at that chap now,” philosophically drawled Stubb, who, with his unlighted short pipe, mechanically retained between his teeth, at a short distance, followed after—“He’s got fits, that Flask has. Fits? yes, give him fits—that’s the very word—pitch fits into ’em. Merrily, merrily, hearts-alive. Pudding for supper, you know;—merry’s the word. Pull, babes—pull, sucklings—pull, all. But what the devil are you hurrying about? Softly, softly, and steadily, my men. Only pull, and keep pulling; nothing more. Crack all your backbones, and bite your knives in two—that’s all. Take it easy—why don’t ye take it easy, I say, and burst all your livers and lungs!”

But what it was that inscrutable Ahab said to that tiger-yellow crew of his—these were words best omitted here; for you live under the blessed light of the evangelical land. Only the infidel sharks in the audacious seas may give ear to such words, when, with tornado brow, and eyes of red murder, and foam-glued lips, Ahab leaped after his prey.

Meanwhile, all the boats tore on. The repeated specific allusions of Flask to “that whale,” as he called the fictitious monster which he declared to be incessantly tantalizing his boat’s bow with its tail—these allusions of his were at times so vivid and life-like, that they would cause some one or two of his men to snatch a fearful look over the shoulder. But this was against all rule; for the oarsmen must put out their eyes, and ram a skewer through their necks; usage pronouncing that they must have no organs but ears, and no limbs but arms, in these critical moments.

It was a sight full of quick wonder and awe! The vast swells of the omnipotent sea; the surging, hollow roar they made, as they rolled along the eight gunwales, like gigantic bowls in a boundless bowling-green; the brief suspended agony of the boat, as it would tip for an instant on the knife-like edge of the sharper waves, that almost seemed threatening to cut it in two; the sudden profound dip into the watery glens and hollows; the keen spurrings and goadings to gain the top of the opposite hill; the headlong, sled-like slide down its other side;—all these, with the cries of the headsmen and harpooneers, and the shuddering gasps of the oarsmen, with the wondrous sight of the ivory Pequod bearing down upon her boats with outstretched sails, like a wild hen after her screaming brood;—all this was thrilling.

Not the raw recruit, marching from the bosom of his wife into the fever heat of his first battle; not the dead man’s ghost encountering the first unknown phantom in the other world;—neither of these can feel stranger and stronger emotions than that man does, who for the first time finds himself pulling into the charmed, churned circle of the hunted sperm whale.

The dancing white water made by the chase was now becoming more and more visible, owing to the increasing darkness of the dun cloud-shadows flung upon the sea. The jets of vapor no longer blended, but tilted everywhere to right and left; the whales seemed separating their wakes. The boats were pulled more apart; Starbuck giving chase to three whales running dead to leeward. Our sail was now set, and, with the still rising wind, we rushed along; the boat going with such madness through the water, that the lee oars could scarcely be worked rapidly enough to escape being torn from the row-locks.
Soon we were running through a suffusing wide veil of mist; neither ship nor boat to be seen.
“Give way, men,” whispered Starbuck, drawing still further aft the sheet of his sail; “there is time to kill a fish yet before the squall comes. There’s white water again!—close to! Spring!”

Soon after, two cries in quick succession on each side of us denoted that the other boats had got fast; but hardly were they overheard, when with a lightning-like hurtling whisper Starbuck said: “Stand up!” and Queequeg, harpoon in hand, sprang to his feet.

Though not one of the oarsmen was then facing the life and death peril so close to them ahead, yet with their eyes on the intense countenance of the mate in the stern of the boat, they knew that the imminent instant had come; they heard, too, an enormous wallowing sound as of fifty elephants stirring in their litter. Meanwhile the boat was still booming through the mist, the waves curling and hissing around us like the erected crests of enraged serpents.
“That’s his hump. There, there, give it to him!” whispered Starbuck.

A short rushing sound leaped out of the boat; it was the darted iron of Queequeg. Then all in one welded commotion came an invisible push from astern, while forward the boat seemed striking on a ledge; the sail collapsed and exploded; a gush of scalding vapor shot up near by; something rolled and tumbled like an earthquake beneath us. The whole crew were half suffocated as they were tossed helter-skelter into the white curdling cream of the squall. Squall, whale, and harpoon had all blended together; and the whale, merely grazed by the iron, escaped.

Though completely swamped, the boat was nearly unharmed. Swimming round it we picked up the floating oars, and lashing them across the gunwale, tumbled back to our places. There we sat up to our knees in the sea, the water covering every rib and plank, so that to our downward gazing eyes the suspended craft seemed a coral boat grown up to us from the bottom of the ocean.

The wind increased to a howl; the waves dashed their bucklers together; the whole squall roared, forked, and crackled around us like a white fire upon the prairie, in which, unconsumed, we were burning; immortal in these jaws of death! In vain we hailed the other boats; as well roar to the live coals down the chimney of a flaming furnace as hail those boats in that storm. Meanwhile the driving scud, rack, and mist, grew darker with the shadows of night; no sign of the ship could be seen. The rising sea forbade all attempts to bale out the boat. The oars were useless as propellers, performing now the office of life-preservers. So, cutting the lashing of the waterproof match keg, after many failures Starbuck contrived to ignite the lamp in the lantern; then stretching it on a waif pole, handed it to Queequeg as the standard-bearer of this forlorn hope. There, then, he sat, holding up that imbecile candle in the heart of that almighty forlornness. There, then, he sat, the sign and symbol of a man without faith, hopelessly holding up hope in the midst of despair.

Wet, drenched through, and shivering cold, despairing of ship or boat, we lifted up our eyes as the dawn came on. The mist still spread over the sea, the empty lantern lay crushed in the bottom of the boat. Suddenly Queequeg started to his feet, hollowing his hand to his ear. We all heard a faint creaking, as of ropes and yards hitherto muffled by the storm. The sound came nearer and nearer; the thick mists were dimly parted by a huge, vague form. Affrighted, we all sprang into the sea as the ship at last loomed into view, bearing right down upon us within a distance of not much more than its length.

Floating on the waves we saw the abandoned boat, as for one instant it tossed and gaped beneath the ship’s bows like a chip at the base of a cataract; and then the vast hull rolled over it, and it was seen no more till it came up weltering astern. Again we swam for it, were dashed against it by the seas, and were at last taken up and safely landed on board. Ere the squall came close to, the other boats had cut loose from their fish and returned to the ship in good time. The ship had given us up, but was still cruising, if haply it might light upon some token of our perishing,—an oar or a lance pole.

“Every man look out along his oars!” cried Starbuck. “Thou, Queequeg, stand up!”

Nimbly springing up on the triangular raised box in the bow, the savage stood erect there, and with intensely eager eyes gazed off towards the spot where the chase had last been descried. Likewise upon the extreme stern of the boat where it was also triangularly platformed level with the gunwale, Starbuck himself was seen coolly and adroitly balancing himself to the jerking tossings of his chip of a craft, and silently eyeing the vast blue eye of the sea.

Not very far distant Flask’s boat was also lying breathlessly still; its commander recklessly standing upon the top of the loggerhead, a stout sort of post rooted in the keel, and rising some two feet above the level of the stern platform. It is used for catching turns with the whale line. Its top is not more spacious than the palm of a man’s hand, and standing upon such a base as that, Flask seemed perched at the mast-head of some ship which had sunk to all but her trucks. But little King-Post was small and short, and at the same time little King-Post was full of a large and tall ambition, so that this loggerhead stand-point of his did by no means satisfy King-Post.
“I can’t see three seas off; tip us up an oar there, and let me on to that.”
Upon this, Daggoo, with either hand upon the gunwale to steady his way, swiftly slid aft, and then erecting himself volunteered his lofty shoulders for a pedestal.
“Good a mast-head as any, sir. Will you mount?”
“That I will, and thank ye very much, my fine fellow; only I wish you fifty feet taller.”

Whereupon planting his feet firmly against two opposite planks of the boat, the gigantic negro, stooping a little, presented his flat palm to Flask’s foot, and then putting Flask’s hand on his hearse-plumed head and bidding him spring as he himself should toss, with one dexterous fling landed the little man high and dry on his shoulders. And here was Flask now standing, Daggoo with one lifted arm furnishing him with a breastband to lean against and steady himself by.

At any time it is a strange sight to the tyro to see with what wondrous habitude of unconscious skill the whaleman will maintain an erect posture in his boat, even when pitched about by the most riotously perverse and cross-running seas. Still more strange to see him giddily perched upon the loggerhead itself, under such circumstances. But the sight of little Flask mounted upon gigantic Daggoo was yet more curious; for sustaining himself with a cool, indifferent, easy, unthought of, barbaric majesty, the noble negro to every roll of the sea harmoniously rolled his fine form. On his broad back, flaxen-haired Flask seemed a snow-flake. The bearer looked nobler than the rider. Though truly vivacious, tumultuous, ostentatious little Flask would now and then stamp with impatience; but not one added heave did he thereby give to the negro’s lordly chest. So have I seen Passion and Vanity stamping the living magnanimous earth, but the earth did not alter her tides and her seasons for that.

Meanwhile Stubb, the third mate, betrayed no such far-gazing solicitudes. The whales might have made one of their regular soundings, not a temporary dive from mere fright; and if that were the case, Stubb, as his wont in such cases, it seems, was resolved to solace the languishing interval with his pipe. He withdrew it from his hatband, where he always wore it aslant like a feather. He loaded it, and rammed home the loading with his thumb-end; but hardly had he ignited his match across the rough sandpaper of his hand, when Tashtego, his harpooneer, whose eyes had been setting to windward like two fixed stars, suddenly dropped like light from his erect attitude to his seat, crying out in a quick phrensy of hurry, “Down, down all, and give way!—there they are!”

To a landsman, no whale, nor any sign of a herring, would have been visible at that moment; nothing but a troubled bit of greenish white water, and thin scattered puffs of vapor hovering over it, and suffusingly blowing off to leeward, like the confused scud from white rolling billows. The air around suddenly vibrated and tingled, as it were, like the air over intensely heated plates of iron. Beneath this atmospheric waving and curling, and partially beneath a thin layer of water, also, the whales were swimming. Seen in advance of all the other indications, the puffs of vapor they spouted, seemed their forerunning couriers and detached flying outriders.

All four boats were now in keen pursuit of that one spot of troubled water and air. But it bade fair to outstrip them; it flew on and on, as a mass of interblending bubbles borne down a rapid stream from the hills.

“Pull, pull, my good boys,” said Starbuck, in the lowest possible but intensest concentrated whisper to his men; while the sharp fixed glance from his eyes darted straight ahead of the bow, almost seemed as two visible needles in two unerring binnacle compasses. He did not say much to his crew, though, nor did his crew say anything to him. Only the silence of the boat was at intervals startlingly pierced by one of his peculiar whispers, now harsh with command, now soft with entreaty.

How different the loud little King-Post. “Sing out and say something, my hearties. Roar and pull, my thunderbolts! Beach me, beach me on their black backs, boys; only do that for me, and I’ll sign over to you my Martha’s Vineyard plantation, boys; including wife and children, boys. Lay me on—lay me on! O Lord, Lord! but I shall go stark, staring mad! See! see that white water!” And so shouting, he pulled his hat from his head, and stamped up and down on it; then picking it up, flirted it far off upon the sea; and finally fell to rearing and plunging in the boat’s stern like a crazed colt from the prairie.

“Look at that chap now,” philosophically drawled Stubb, who, with his unlighted short pipe, mechanically retained between his teeth, at a short distance, followed after—“He’s got fits, that Flask has. Fits? yes, give him fits—that’s the very word—pitch fits into ’em. Merrily, merrily, hearts-alive. Pudding for supper, you know;—merry’s the word. Pull, babes—pull, sucklings—pull, all. But what the devil are you hurrying about? Softly, softly, and steadily, my men. Only pull, and keep pulling; nothing more. Crack all your backbones, and bite your knives in two—that’s all. Take it easy—why don’t ye take it easy, I say, and burst all your livers and lungs!”

But what it was that inscrutable Ahab said to that tiger-yellow crew of his—these were words best omitted here; for you live under the blessed light of the evangelical land. Only the infidel sharks in the audacious seas may give ear to such words, when, with tornado brow, and eyes of red murder, and foam-glued lips, Ahab leaped after his prey.

Meanwhile, all the boats tore on. The repeated specific allusions of Flask to “that whale,” as he called the fictitious monster which he declared to be incessantly tantalizing his boat’s bow with its tail—these allusions of his were at times so vivid and life-like, that they would cause some one or two of his men to snatch a fearful look over the shoulder. But this was against all rule; for the oarsmen must put out their eyes, and ram a skewer through their necks; usage pronouncing that they must have no organs but ears, and no limbs but arms, in these critical moments.

It was a sight full of quick wonder and awe! The vast swells of the omnipotent sea; the surging, hollow roar they made, as they rolled along the eight gunwales, like gigantic bowls in a boundless bowling-green; the brief suspended agony of the boat, as it would tip for an instant on the knife-like edge of the sharper waves, that almost seemed threatening to cut it in two; the sudden profound dip into the watery glens and hollows; the keen spurrings and goadings to gain the top of the opposite hill; the headlong, sled-like slide down its other side;—all these, with the cries of the headsmen and harpooneers, and the shuddering gasps of the oarsmen, with the wondrous sight of the ivory Pequod bearing down upon her boats with outstretched sails, like a wild hen after her screaming brood;—all this was thrilling.

Not the raw recruit, marching from the bosom of his wife into the fever heat of his first battle; not the dead man’s ghost encountering the first unknown phantom in the other world;—neither of these can feel stranger and stronger emotions than that man does, who for the first time finds himself pulling into the charmed, churned circle of the hunted sperm whale.

The dancing white water made by the chase was now becoming more and more visible, owing to the increasing darkness of the dun cloud-shadows flung upon the sea. The jets of vapor no longer blended, but tilted everywhere to right and left; the whales seemed separating their wakes. The boats were pulled more apart; Starbuck giving chase to three whales running dead to leeward. Our sail was now set, and, with the still rising wind, we rushed along; the boat going with such madness through the water, that the lee oars could scarcely be worked rapidly enough to escape being torn from the row-locks.
Soon we were running through a suffusing wide veil of mist; neither ship nor boat to be seen.
“Give way, men,” whispered Starbuck, drawing still further aft the sheet of his sail; “there is time to kill a fish yet before the squall comes. There’s white water again!—close to! Spring!”

Soon after, two cries in quick succession on each side of us denoted that the other boats had got fast; but hardly were they overheard, when with a lightning-like hurtling whisper Starbuck said: “Stand up!” and Queequeg, harpoon in hand, sprang to his feet.

Though not one of the oarsmen was then facing the life and death peril so close to them ahead, yet with their eyes on the intense countenance of the mate in the stern of the boat, they knew that the imminent instant had come; they heard, too, an enormous wallowing sound as of fifty elephants stirring in their litter. Meanwhile the boat was still booming through the mist, the waves curling and hissing around us like the erected crests of enraged serpents.
“That’s his hump. _There_, _there_, give it to him!” whispered Starbuck.

A short rushing sound leaped out of the boat; it was the darted iron of Queequeg. Then all in one welded commotion came an invisible push from astern, while forward the boat seemed striking on a ledge; the sail collapsed and exploded; a gush of scalding vapor shot up near by; something rolled and tumbled like an earthquake beneath us. The whole crew were half suffocated as they were tossed helter-skelter into the white curdling cream of the squall. Squall, whale, and harpoon had all blended together; and the whale, merely grazed by the iron, escaped.

Though completely swamped, the boat was nearly unharmed. Swimming round it we picked up the floating oars, and lashing them across the gunwale, tumbled back to our places. There we sat up to our knees in the sea, the water covering every rib and plank, so that to our downward gazing eyes the suspended craft seemed a coral boat grown up to us from the bottom of the ocean.

The wind increased to a howl; the waves dashed their bucklers together; the whole squall roared, forked, and crackled around us like a white fire upon the prairie, in which, unconsumed, we were burning; immortal in these jaws of death! In vain we hailed the other boats; as well roar to the live coals down the chimney of a flaming furnace as hail those boats in that storm. Meanwhile the driving scud, rack, and mist, grew darker with the shadows of night; no sign of the ship could be seen. The rising sea forbade all attempts to bale out the boat. The oars were useless as propellers, performing now the office of life-preservers. So, cutting the lashing of the waterproof match keg, after many failures Starbuck contrived to ignite the lamp in the lantern; then stretching it on a waif pole, handed it to Queequeg as the standard-bearer of this forlorn hope. There, then, he sat, holding up that imbecile candle in the heart of that almighty forlornness. There, then, he sat, the sign and symbol of a man without faith, hopelessly holding up hope in the midst of despair.

Wet, drenched through, and shivering cold, despairing of ship or boat, we lifted up our eyes as the dawn came on. The mist still spread over the sea, the empty lantern lay crushed in the bottom of the boat. Suddenly Queequeg started to his feet, hollowing his hand to his ear. We all heard a faint creaking, as of ropes and yards hitherto muffled by the storm. The sound came nearer and nearer; the thick mists were dimly parted by a huge, vague form. Affrighted, we all sprang into the sea as the ship at last loomed into view, bearing right down upon us within a distance of not much more than its length.

Floating on the waves we saw the abandoned boat, as for one instant it tossed and gaped beneath the ship’s bows like a chip at the base of a cataract; and then the vast hull rolled over it, and it was seen no more till it came up weltering astern. Again we swam for it, were dashed against it by the seas, and were at last taken up and safely landed on board. Ere the squall came close to, the other boats had cut loose from their fish and returned to the ship in good time. The ship had given us up, but was still cruising, if haply it might light upon some token of our perishing,—an oar or a lance pole.

paragraphs: The phantoms, for so they seemed at the time, were flitting on the other side of the deck, and with a noiseless swiftness were casting loose the tackles and bands of the boat that hung there. This boat had always been considered one of the spare boats, though technically it was called the captain's, because it hung from the starboard quarter. The figure that now stood by its bow was tall and dark, with one white tooth evilly protruding from his steel-like lips. A rumpled Chinese jacket of black cotton clothed him funereally, with wide black trousers of the same dark stuff. But strangely crowning all this blackness was a glistening white plaited turban — his own living hair, braided and coiled round and round upon his head. Less dark in appearance, the companions of this figure had that vivid, tiger-yellow complexion peculiar to some of the aboriginal natives of the Manila islands — a race notorious for a certain devilish subtlety, and supposed by some honest white sailors to be the paid spies and secret confidential agents, here on the water, of their lord the devil, whose counting-room they suppose to be elsewhere.
While the wondering ship's company were still staring at these strangers, Ahab cried out to the white-turbaned old man at their head, "All ready there, Fedallah?"
"Ready," was the half-hissed reply.
"Lower away then, do you hear?" he shouted across the deck. "Lower away there, I say."

Such was the thunder of his voice that, despite their amazement, the men sprang over the rail. The pulleys whirled round in the blocks. With a lurch, the three boats dropped into the sea. And with a deft, offhand daring unknown in any other profession, the sailors leaped like goats down the rolling ship's side into the tossing boats below.

They had hardly pulled out from under the ship's shelter when a fourth boat, coming from the windward side, pulled around under the stern and revealed the five strangers rowing Ahab, who stood erect in the stern and loudly ordered Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask to spread themselves widely so as to cover a large stretch of water. But with all their eyes riveted upon the dark Fedallah and his crew, the men in the other boats did not obey the command.
"Captain Ahab? —" said Starbuck.
"Spread yourselves," cried Ahab. "Give way, all four boats. You, Flask, pull out more to leeward!"

"Aye, aye, sir," cheerily cried little King-Post, sweeping his great steering oar around. "Lay back!" he called to his crew. "There! — there! — there again! There she blows right ahead, boys! — lay back!"
"Never mind those yellow fellows, Archy."
"Oh, I don't mind them, sir," said Archy. "I knew it all before. Didn't I hear them in the hold? And didn't I tell Cabaco here about it? What do you say, Cabaco? They are stowaways, Mr. Flask."

"Pull, pull, my fine hearts-alive; pull, my children; pull, my little ones," Stubb sighed to his crew in a slow, soothing drawl, some of them still showing signs of uneasiness. "Why don't you break your backbones, my boys? What is it you're staring at? Those chaps in that boat over there? Tut! They are only five more hands come to help us — never mind from where — the more the merrier. Pull, then, do pull; never mind the brimstone — devils are good enough fellows. So, so; there you are now; that's the stroke for a thousand pounds; that's the stroke to sweep the stakes! Hurrah for the gold cup of sperm oil, my heroes! Three cheers, men — all hearts alive! Easy, easy; don't be in a hurry — don't be in a hurry. Why don't you snap your oars, you rascals? Bite something, you dogs! So, so, so, then — softly, softly! That's it — that's it! Long and strong. Give way there, give way! The devil take you, you ragamuffin rapscallions; you're all asleep. Stop snoring, you sleepers, and pull. Pull, will you? Pull, can't you? Pull, won't you? Why in the name of gudgeons and ginger-cakes don't you pull? — pull and break something! Pull, till your eyes start out of your head! Here!" — whipping the sharp knife out of his belt — "every mother's son of you draw his knife, and pull with the blade between his teeth. That's it — that's it. Now you're doing something; that looks like it, my steel-bits. Start her — start her, my silver-spoons! Start her, marling-spikes!"

Stubb's opening address to his crew is given here in full because he had rather a peculiar way of talking to them in general, and especially in preaching the religion of rowing. But you must not suppose from this sample of his sermons that he ever flew into real rages with his congregation. Not at all — and that was his chief peculiarity. He would say the most terrible things to his crew in a tone so strangely mixed of fun and fury, with the fury seeming so calculated merely as a spice to the fun, that no oarsman could hear such odd invocations without pulling for dear life, and yet pulling for the mere joke of the thing. Besides, all the while he himself looked so easy and lazy, handled his steering-oar so loungingly, and yawned so broadly — open-mouthed at times — that the mere sight of such a yawning commander, by sheer force of contrast, worked like a charm upon the crew. Then again, Stubb was one of those odd sorts of humorists whose jollity is sometimes so curiously ambiguous as to put all their subordinates on guard when it comes to obeying them.
In obedience to a signal from Ahab, Starbuck was now pulling diagonally across Stubb's bow. When for a minute or so the two boats were fairly near each other, Stubb hailed the mate.
"Mr. Starbuck! Portside boat there, ahoy! A word with you, sir, if you please!"
"Hello!" returned Starbuck, turning not a single inch as he spoke, still earnestly but in whispers urging his crew, his face set like flint away from Stubb's.
"What do you think of those yellow fellows, sir?"

"Smuggled on board, somehow, before the ship sailed. (Strong, strong, boys!)" in a whisper to his crew, then speaking out loud again: "A sad business, Mr. Stubb! (Drive her, drive her, my lads!) But never mind, Mr. Stubb, all for the best. Let all your crew pull strong, come what may. (Spring, my men, spring!) There's hogsheads of sperm ahead, Mr. Stubb, and that's what you came for. (Pull, my boys!) Sperm, sperm's the game! This at least is duty — duty and profit hand in hand."

"Aye, aye, I thought as much," Stubb said to himself when the boats diverged. "As soon as I clapped eyes on them, I thought so. Aye, and that's what he went into the after-hold for so often, as Dough-Boy long suspected. They were hidden down there. The White Whale's at the bottom of it. Well, well, so be it! Can't be helped! All right! Give way, men! It isn't the White Whale today! Give way!"

Now, the arrival of these outlandish strangers at such a critical moment as the lowering of the boats had, not unreasonably, stirred a kind of superstitious amazement in some of the ship's company. But Archy's supposed discovery had got around among them some time before, and though nobody had believed it then, it had in some small measure prepared them for the event. It took the sharpest edge off their wonder; and so, what with all this and Stubb's confident way of accounting for the strangers' appearance, they were for the time freed from superstitious guessing — though the affair still left plenty of room for all kinds of wild conjectures about dark Ahab's exact part in the matter from the beginning. As for me, I silently recalled the mysterious shadows I had seen creeping on board the Pequod in the dim Nantucket dawn, as well as the cryptic hints of the unaccountable Elijah.

Meanwhile Ahab, out of hearing of his officers, having edged farthest to windward, was still ranging ahead of the other boats — a sign of how powerful a crew was pulling him. Those tiger-yellow creatures of his seemed all steel and whalebone. "I can't see three waves off. Tip us up an oar there and let me climb on that."

"Give way, men," whispered Starbuck, drawing the sheet of his sail still further aft. "There is time to kill a fish yet before the squall comes. There's white water again! — close by! Spring!"

Soon after, two cries in quick succession on each side of us told us the other boats had struck fast. But they were hardly heard when, with a lightning-fast hissing whisper, Starbuck said: "Stand up!" and Queequeg, harpoon in hand, sprang to his feet.

Though not one of the oarsmen was facing the life-and-death danger so close ahead, yet with their eyes on the intense face of the mate in the stern of the boat, they knew the critical instant had come. They heard, too, an enormous wallowing sound, as of fifty elephants stirring in their bedding. Meanwhile the boat was still racing through the mist, the waves curling and hissing around us like the raised crests of enraged serpents.
"That's his hump. There, there, give it to him!" whispered Starbuck.

A short rushing sound leaped out of the boat — it was the darted iron of Queequeg. Then all in one welded commotion came an invisible push from behind, while forward the boat seemed to strike a ledge. The sail collapsed and exploded. A gush of scalding vapor shot up nearby. Something rolled and tumbled like an earthquake beneath us. The whole crew was half-suffocated as they were tossed helter-skelter into the white curdling cream of the squall. Squall, whale, and harpoon had all blended together. And the whale, merely grazed by the iron, escaped.

The boat was completely swamped but almost undamaged. We swam around it and gathered up the floating oars, lashed them across the gunwale, and scrambled back into our places. There we sat, knee-deep in the sea, with water over every rib and plank, so that to our eyes, gazing down, the boat hanging there in the water seemed like a coral boat that had grown up to us from the ocean floor.

The wind increased to a howl; the waves clashed their shields together; the whole squall roared, forked, and crackled around us like a white fire on the prairie, in which we were burning without being consumed — immortal in these jaws of death! In vain we hailed the other boats; you might as well roar to the live coals down the chimney of a blazing furnace as hail those boats in that storm. Meanwhile the driving spray, flying cloud, and mist grew darker with the shadows of night; no sign of the ship could be seen. The rising sea ruled out any attempt to bail out the boat. The oars were useless for rowing, and now served as life-preservers. So, cutting the lashing of the waterproof match keg, Starbuck, after many failures, managed to light the lamp in the lantern; then, fixing it on a waif pole (the flagged pole used to mark a killed whale), he handed it to Queequeg as the standard-bearer of this forlorn hope. There, then, he sat, holding up that feeble candle in the heart of that almighty forlornness. There, then, he sat, the sign and symbol of a man without faith, hopelessly holding up hope in the midst of despair.

Wet and drenched through, shivering with cold, having given up hope of either ship or boat, we raised our eyes as dawn broke. The mist still lay spread over the sea, and the empty lantern lay crushed in the bottom of the boat. Suddenly Queequeg leaped to his feet and cupped his hand to his ear. We all heard a faint creaking, like the sound of ropes and yards that the storm had muffled until now. It came closer and closer; a huge, vague shape dimly parted the thick mist. In terror we all jumped into the sea as the ship finally loomed into view, bearing straight down on us, hardly more than her own length away.

From where we floated in the waves we saw the abandoned boat toss and gape for one instant under the ship's bows, like a chip of wood at the foot of a waterfall; then the huge hull rolled over it, and it vanished until it surfaced again, wallowing, astern. We swam for it again, were flung against it by the seas, and were finally picked up and brought safely on board. The other boats had cut loose from their fish before the squall reached them and had got back to the ship in good time. The ship had given us up for lost but was still cruising about, in case it might happen upon some sign of our death — an oar or a lance pole.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 48 — Den Første Udsætning
paragraphs: Genfærdene, for sådan så de ud i øjeblikket, svævede rundt på den anden side af dækket og løsnede lydløst og hurtigt taljerne og båndene på den båd, der hang dér. Den båd havde altid været regnet for en af reservebådene, selv om den formelt blev kaldt kaptajnens, fordi den hang på styrbords agterkvarter. Skikkelsen, der nu stod ved dens stævn, var høj og mørk, med én hvid tand, der ondskabsfuldt stak frem mellem de stålagtige læber. En krøllet kinesisk jakke af sort bomuld klædte ham som i sorg, med vide sorte bukser af samme mørke stof. Men besynderligt nok kronede en skinnende hvid flettet turban hele denne sorthed — hans eget levende hår, flettet og rullet rundt og rundt oppe på hovedet. Mindre mørke at se på var denne skikkelses følgesvende, der havde den friske, tigergule hudfarve, som er særlig for nogle af de oprindelige indbyggere på Manila-øerne — et folk, der er berygtet for en vis djævelsk snuhed, og som nogle ærlige hvide sømænd tror er deres herres, djævelens, betalte spioner og hemmelige fortrolige agenter her på havet, mens hans kontor, tror de, ligger et andet sted.
Mens skibets forbløffede mandskab endnu stirrede på de fremmede, råbte Ahab til den hvidturbanerede gamle mand i spidsen for dem: »Er I klar derovre, Fedallah?«
»Klar,« lød det halvt hvislende svar.
»Så fir ned, hører I?« råbte han hen over dækket. »Fir ned dér, siger jeg.«

Hans stemme lød som torden, så mændene sprang over rælingen, trods deres forbløffelse. Blokkenes hjul snurrede rundt. Med et ryk faldt de tre både ned i havet. Og med en let, ligeglad dristighed, som ikke kendes i noget andet fag, sprang sømændene som bjergged ned ad skibssiden, der rullede, ned i de dansende både under dem.

De var næppe kommet ud fra skibets læ, da en fjerde båd fra luvsiden roede om under hækken og afslørede de fem fremmede, der roede Ahab. Han stod oprejst i agterenden og beordrede højlydt Starbuck, Stubb og Flask til at sprede sig vidt, så de dækkede et stort stykke hav. Men med alle øjne limet til den mørke Fedallah og hans mandskab adlød mændene i de andre både ikke ordren.
»Kaptajn Ahab? —« sagde Starbuck.
»Spred jer,« råbte Ahab. »Læg jer i årerne, alle fire både. Du, Flask, ro længere ud mod læ!«

»Javel, sir,« råbte lille King-Post muntert og svingede sin store styreåre rundt. »Læg jer i!« råbte han til sin besætning. »Sådan! — sådan! — sådan igen! Der blæser hun lige forude, drenge! — læg jer i!«
»Lad være med at tænke på de gule fyre, Archy.«

»Åh, jeg tænker ikke på dem, sir,« sagde Archy. »Jeg vidste det hele i forvejen. Hørte jeg dem ikke nede i lasten? Og fortalte jeg ikke Cabaco her om det? Hvad siger du, Cabaco? De er blinde passagerer, Mr. Flask.«

»Træk, træk, mine kære gutter; træk, mine børn; træk, mine små,« sukkede Stubb til sin besætning i en langsom, beroligende sløv tone, for nogle af dem viste stadig tegn på uro. »Hvorfor knækker I ikke ryggen, drenge? Hvad stirrer I på? På de fyre i den båd derovre? Pyt! De er bare fem hænder mere, der er kommet for at hjælpe os — lige meget hvorfra — jo flere, jo bedre. Træk så, træk dog; glem alt om svovlen — djævle er gode nok fyre. Sådan, sådan; så er det; det er årtaget, der er tusind pund værd; det er årtaget, der tager hele potten! Hurra for den gyldne pokal af spermolie, mine helte! Tre hurraer, mænd — alle hjerter levende! Rolig, rolig; ingen hast — ingen hast. Hvorfor knækker I ikke årerne, slubberter? Bid i noget, hunde! Sådan, sådan, sådan så — stille, stille! Det er det — det er det! Langt og kraftigt. Læg jer i dér, læg jer i! Fanden tage jer, jeres pjaltede slyngler; I sover alle sammen. Hold op med at snorke, sovehoveder, og træk. Træk, vil I? Træk, kan I ikke? Træk, gider I ikke? Hvorfor i alverden, ved grundlinger og honningkager, trækker I ikke? — træk og knæk noget! Træk, til øjnene springer ud af hovedet på jer! Her!« — og han rev den skarpe kniv ud af bæltet — »hver eneste mors dreng af jer trækker sin kniv og trækker med bladet mellem tænderne. Sådan, sådan. Nu gør I noget; det ligner noget, mine stålmunde. Kom i gang med hende — kom i gang, mine sølvskeer! Kom i gang med hende, splejsenåle!«

Stubbs indledende tale til sin besætning er gengivet her i sin helhed, fordi han havde en ret særlig måde at tale til dem på i almindelighed, og især når han prædikede roningens religion. Men man må ikke tro ud fra denne prøve på hans prædikener, at han nogensinde fik virkelige raserianfald over for sin menighed. Slet ikke — og det var hans fornemste ejendommelighed. Han kunne sige de mest forfærdelige ting til sin besætning i en tone, der var så besynderligt blandet af løjer og vrede, og hvor vreden så så beregnet ud som blot krydderi til løjerne, at ingen roer kunne høre sådanne mærkelige besværgelser uden at trække for livet, og alligevel trække bare for spøgens skyld. Desuden så han hele tiden selv så rolig og sløv ud, håndterede sin styreåre så henslængt og gabte så højt — nogle gange med vidt åben mund — at synet af sådan en gabende fører, ved ren kontrastvirkning, virkede som en besværgelse på mandskabet. Og så var Stubb også en af de sære slags spøgefugle, hvis munterhed er så mærkeligt tvetydig, at alle deres underordnede er på vagt, når det gælder om at adlyde dem.
På et tegn fra Ahab roede Starbuck nu på skrå på tværs af Stubbs stævn. Da de to både et minuts tid var ret tæt på hinanden, råbte Stubb til styrmanden.
»Mr. Starbuck! Båden på bagbord, ohøj! Et ord med Dem, sir, hvis De vil være så venlig!«
»Hallo!« svarede Starbuck uden at dreje sig en tomme, mens han talte, og han opmuntrede stadig inderligt, men hviskende, sin besætning med ansigtet stift som flint vendt væk fra Stubbs.
»Hvad synes De om de gule fyre, sir?«

»Smuglet om bord på en eller anden måde, før skibet sejlede. (Kraftigt, kraftigt, drenge!)« hviskede han til sin besætning og talte så højt igen: »Det er en sørgelig sag, Mr. Stubb! (Driv hende frem, driv hende frem, mine knægte!) Men lad være, Mr. Stubb, alt er til det bedste. Lad hele jeres besætning trække kraftigt, hvad der end sker. (Spring, mine mænd, spring!) Der er tønder fulde af spermolie forude, Mr. Stubb, og det er det, De kom for. (Træk, mine drenge!) Sperm, sperm er det, det gælder! Det her er i det mindste pligt — pligt og fortjeneste hånd i hånd.«

»Javel, det tænkte jeg nok,« sagde Stubb til sig selv, da bådene skiltes. »Så snart jeg fik øje på dem, tænkte jeg det. Ja, og det er det, han så ofte gik ind i agterlasten efter, som Dough-Boy længe har mistænkt. De var skjult dernede. Den Hvide Hval er årsagen til det hele. Nå, nå, lad gå! Det kan ikke hjælpes! Godt så! Læg jer i, mænd! Det er ikke den Hvide Hval i dag! Læg jer i!«

Nu havde de sære fremmedes ankomst i et så afgørende øjeblik som nedfiringen af bådene med god grund vakt en slags overtroisk forbløffelse hos nogle af skibets folk. Men Archys påståede opdagelse var kommet rundt blandt dem nogen tid i forvejen, og selv om ingen dengang havde troet på den, havde den i nogen grad forberedt dem på begivenheden. Det tog den skarpeste kant af deres undren; og så, hvad med alt dette og Stubbs selvsikre måde at forklare de fremmedes tilsynekomst på, var de for en tid fri for overtroisk gætteri — selv om sagen stadig levnede rigeligt rum for alle slags vilde formodninger om den mørke Ahabs nøjagtige rolle i sagen fra begyndelsen. Hvad mig angik, huskede jeg stille de mystiske skygger, jeg havde set liste sig ombord på Pequod i det svage daggry i Nantucket, og de gådefulde antydninger fra den uforklarlige Elijah.

Imens var Ahab, uden for hørevidde af sine styrmænd, roet længst mod luv og trak stadig foran de andre både — et tegn på, hvor stærk en besætning der roede ham. Hans tigergule folk så ud, som om de var af rent stål og hvalbarder. Som fem faldhammere steg og faldt de i jævne, kraftige tag, som med jævne mellemrum skød båden hen over vandet som en liggende sprængt kedel ud af en Mississippi-damper. Fedallah, der sås ved harpunerens åre, havde kastet sin sorte jakke og blottet brystet, hele hans krop over dollbordet tydeligt aftegnet mod de skiftende dyk af den vandige horisont; mens Ahab i den anden ende af båden, med den ene arm kastet halvt bagud i luften som en fægters, som for at veje op mod enhver tilbøjelighed til at snuble, sås at styre sin styreåre roligt, som han havde gjort tusind gange ved nedfiring af både, før Den Hvide Hval rev ham itu. Med ét lavede den udstrakte arm en ejendommelig bevægelse og blev så stående, mens bådens fem årer alle på én gang sås løftet lodret. Båd og besætning sad ubevægelige på havet. Straks standsede de tre spredte både bagved på deres vej. Hvalerne var uregelmæssigt sunket helt ned i det blå uden at give noget tegn på bevægelsen, som kunne ses på afstand, selv om Ahab, der var tættere på, havde set den.
»Hver mand holder udkig langs sin åre!« råbte Starbuck. »Du, Queequeg, rejs dig op!«

Queequeg sprang adræt op på den trekantede forhøjede kasse i stævnen, og vilden stod der oprejst og stirrede med intenst ivrige øjne hen mod stedet, hvor jagten sidst var set. På samme måde sås Starbuck selv helt ude agter i båden, hvor den også var bygget op til en trekantet platform i højde med dollbordet, koldt og dygtigt at holde balancen mod de ryk og stød fra hans lille skal af et fartøj, mens han tavst spejdede ud over havets store blå øje.

Ikke ret langt væk lå også Flasks båd åndeløst stille. Dens fører stod letsindigt oppe på loggerheaden, en kraftig slags pæl, der er rodfæstet i kølen og rager omkring to fod op over agterplatformens niveau. Den bruges til at tage bugter på hvallinen. Dens top er ikke større end en mands håndflade, og stående på sådan et fodfæste så Flask ud, som om han sad på mastetoppen af et skib, der var sunket, så kun hendes mastekapper stak op, kapperne allerøverst på masterne. Men lille King-Post var lille og kort, og samtidig var lille King-Post fuld af en stor og høj ærgerrighed, så dette loggerhead-udsigtspunkt tilfredsstillede på ingen måde King-Post.
»Jeg kan ikke se tre bølger frem. Hold en åre op her og lad mig kravle op på den.«
Så gled Daggoo, med begge hænder på dollbordet for at holde balancen, hurtigt ned til agterenden, rettede sig så op og tilbød sine høje skuldre som fodstykke.
»Så god en mastetop som nogen, sir. Vil De stige op?«
»Det vil jeg gerne, og mange tak, min gode ven. Jeg ville bare ønske, at du var halvtreds fod højere.«

Hvorpå den kæmpestore sorte mand satte fødderne fast mod to modstående planker i båden, bøjede sig lidt og rakte sin flade håndflade frem til Flasks fod; så lagde han Flasks hånd på sit hoved med ligfærdsfjer og bad ham springe lige i det øjeblik, han selv kastede, og med ét behændigt sving landede han den lille mand højt og tørt på sine skuldre. Og nu stod Flask her, mens Daggoo med den ene løftede arm gav ham et brystværn at læne sig op ad og støtte sig til.

Det er til enhver tid et mærkeligt syn for nybegynderen at se, med hvilken forunderlig, ubevidst vane for dygtighed hvalfangeren holder sig oprejst i sin båd, selv når den kastes rundt af de mest ustyrligt genstridige og krydsende søer. Mærkeligere endnu er det at se ham svimlende siddende på selve loggerheaden under sådanne forhold. Men synet af lille Flask, stående oven på den kæmpestore Daggoo, var endnu mere sælsomt; for mens den ædle sorte mand holdt sig oprejst med en kold, ligeglad, let, utvungen, barbarisk majestæt, rullede han sin fine skikkelse i takt med hver rulning af havet. På hans brede ryg lignede den lyshårede Flask et snefnug. Bæreren så ædlere ud end rytteren. Det er sandt, at den livlige, støjende, pralende lille Flask nu og da stampede utålmodigt; men han tilføjede ikke et eneste løft til den sortes fyrstelige bryst ved det. Sådan har jeg set Lidenskab og Forfængelighed stampe på den levende, storsindede jord, men jorden ændrede ikke sine tidevand og årstider for det.

Imens viste Stubb, den tredje styrmand, ingen sådan angst for at spejde langt væk. Hvalerne havde måske foretaget en af deres almindelige sænkninger (de lange, dybe dyk) og ikke et kort dyk af ren skræk. Og hvis det var tilfældet, var Stubb, som det åbenbart var hans vane i den slags tilfælde, fast besluttet på at fordrive den sløve ventetid med sin pibe. Han tog den frem fra hattebåndet, hvor han altid bar den på skrå som en fjer. Han stoppede den og pressede tobakken ned med enden af tommelfingeren. Men han havde knapt nok strøget tændstikken over sin hånds ru sandpapir, før Tashtego, hans harpuner, hvis øjne havde været vendt mod luv som to faste stjerner, pludselig faldt som et lys fra sin oprejste stilling ned på sit sæde og råbte i en hurtig, hektisk hast: »Ned, ned alle sammen, og tag årerne! — der er de!«

For en landkrabbe ville ingen hval, ja ikke så meget som en sild, have været at se i det øjeblik — kun en urolig plet grønhvidt vand med tynde, spredte stråler af damp svævende over og drivende ud i alle retninger mod læ, som det forvirrede stænk fra hvide rullende brændinger. Luften rundt om dirrede og prikkede pludselig, så at sige, som luften over stærkt opvarmede jernplader. Under denne bølgen og krusen i luften, og delvis også under et tyndt lag vand, svømmede hvalerne. Set foran alle de andre tegn lignede de dampstråler, de sprøjtede op, deres kurérer, der løb i forvejen, deres udsendte forridere, der fløj forud.

Alle fire både var nu i ivrig jagt efter det ene sted med uroligt vand og urolig luft. Men det så ud til at ville løbe fra dem. Det fløj videre og videre som en klump af sammenflydende bobler, der skylles ned ad en hurtig bjergå.

»Træk, træk, mine gode drenge,« sagde Starbuck i den lavest mulige, men mest intenst koncentrerede hvisken til sine folk. Det skarpe, faste blik fra hans øjne, rettet lige frem forbi stævnen, lignede næsten to synlige nåle i to ufejlbarlige kompashuse. Han sagde ikke meget til sine folk, og de sagde heller ikke noget til ham. Kun af og til blev bådens stilhed skærende brudt af en af hans særegne hviskninger — nu hård af kommando, nu blød af bøn.

Hvor anderledes den højrøstede lille King-Post. »Råb op og sig noget, mine gutter! Brøl og træk, mine tordenskrald! Sæt mig op, sæt mig op på deres sorte rygge, drenge! Bare gør det for mig, så skriver jeg min plantage på Martha's Vineyard over til jer, drenge — med kone og børn, drenge! Læg mig an — læg mig an! Åh Herre, Herre! Jeg bliver splittergal! Se! Se det hvide vand!« Og mens han råbte sådan, rev han hatten af hovedet og trampede op og ned på den. Så tog han den op og slyngede den langt ud over havet. Til sidst begyndte han at stejle og buldre i bådens agterende som et skør føl fra prærien.

»Se lige på ham nu,« sagde Stubb træg og filosofisk, mens han fulgte med et lille stykke bagefter med sin utændte pibe stadig mekanisk klemt mellem tænderne. »Han har anfald, den Flask. Anfald? Ja, giv ham anfald — det er netop ordet — kast anfald i dem. Muntert, muntert, gutter! Budding til aftensmad, ved I — muntert er ordet. Træk, babyer — træk, pattebørn — træk, alle sammen. Men hvad fanden haster I efter? Stille, stille og jævnt, mine mænd. Bare træk, og bliv ved med at trække. Ikke andet. Knæk alle jeres rygge, og bid jeres knive over — det er det hele. Tag det roligt — hvorfor tager I det ikke roligt, siger jeg, og sprænger alle jeres lever og lunger!«

Men hvad den uransagelige Ahab sagde til sit tigergule mandskab — de ord er bedst at udelade her, for I lever under det velsignede lys i et evangelisk land. Kun de vantro hajer i de dristige have må høre den slags ord, når Ahab med en tornadopande og øjne af rødt mord og skumlimede læber sprang efter sit bytte.

Imens fløj alle bådene videre. Flasks gentagne, bestemte henvisninger til »den hval«, som han kaldte det indbildte uhyre, han påstod hele tiden drillede bådens stævn med halen — disse henvisninger var til tider så levende og livagtige, at de fik en eller to af hans folk til at kaste et skræmt blik over skulderen. Men det var imod alle regler, for roerne må stikke deres øjne ud og stikke en spids pind gennem nakken, da skikken siger, at de i disse afgørende øjeblikke ikke må have andre organer end ører og ingen andre lemmer end arme.

Det var et syn fuldt af hurtig undren og ærefrygt! De vældige dønninger fra det almægtige hav. Det bølgende, hule brøl, de lavede, mens de rullede langs de otte rælinger som gigantiske kugler på en grænseløs kegleplæne. Bådens korte, svævende kval, når den et øjeblik vippede på de skarpere bølgers knivsæg, som næsten syntes at true med at skære den over. Det pludselige dybe dyk ned i de vandige dale og lavninger. Det skarpe spore og drive for at nå toppen af den modsatte bakke. Det hovedkulds slædeglid ned ad dens anden side — alt dette sammen med råbene fra styrmændene og harpunererne og roernes skælvende gisp og det forunderlige syn af det elfenbenshvide Pequod, der stod ned mod sine både med udstrakte sejl som en vild høne efter sin skrigende kyllingeflok — alt dette var spændende.

Ikke den uerfarne rekrut, der marcherer direkte fra sin hustrus arme ind i febervarmen i sit første slag. Ikke den dødes genfærd, der møder den anden verdens første ukendte spøgelse. Ingen af dem føler mærkeligere eller stærkere følelser end den mand, der for første gang finder sig roende ind i den fortryllede, oprørte kreds om en jaget kaskelot.

Det dansende hvide vand, som jagten piskede op, blev mere og mere synligt nu, fordi de matte skyskygger på havet blev mørkere. Dampstrålerne var holdt op med at flyde sammen og skrånede i alle retninger, til højre og venstre. Hvalerne syntes at dele deres kølvand i stykker. Bådene spredte sig længere fra hinanden, og Starbuck satte efter tre hvaler, der løb lige mod læ. Vi havde vores sejl sat nu, og med vinden stadig stigende fløj vi af sted, mens båden rev gennem vandet så vanvittigt, at læsidens årer næsten ikke kunne holdes i gang hurtigt nok til at undgå at blive revet ud af dollerne.
Snart løb vi gennem et bredt, drivende slør af tåge. Hverken skib eller båd at se.
»Træk til, mænd,« hviskede Starbuck og trak sin sejlskøde endnu længere agterud. »Der er tid til at dræbe en fisk endnu, før stormbygen kommer. Der er hvidt vand igen! — tæt på! Spring til!«

Kort efter fortalte to råb i hurtig rækkefølge på hver side af os, at de andre både havde fået fast. Men de var knapt nok hørt, da Starbuck med en lynhurtigt hvislende hvisken sagde: »Rejs dig!« og Queequeg, med harpunen i hånden, sprang op på benene.

Selv om ikke en eneste af roerne vendte ansigtet mod livsfaren så tæt forude, vidste de alligevel, med øjnene på styrmandens anspændte ansigt agter i båden, at det afgørende øjeblik var kommet. De hørte også en enorm vælten sig rundt, som af halvtreds elefanter, der rørte på sig i deres leje. Imens fløj båden stadig gennem tågen, og bølgerne krøllede og hvislede rundt om os som de rejste kamme på vrede slanger.
»Det er hans pukkel. Der, der, giv ham den!« hviskede Starbuck.

En kort susende lyd sprang ud af båden — det var Queequegs kastede jern. Så kom, i ét sammensmeltet oprør, et usynligt puf bagfra, mens båden forude syntes at ramme en afsats. Sejlet klappede sammen og sprang i stykker. En byge af skoldende damp skød op tæt ved. Noget rullede og væltede som et jordskælv under os. Hele besætningen var halvt kvalt, mens de blev kastet hulter til bulter ind i stormbygens hvide, stivnende fløde. Bygen, hvalen og harpunen var alle smeltet sammen. Og hvalen, som jernet kun lige havde strejfet, slap væk.

Båden var fuldstændig fyldt med vand, men næsten uden skade. Vi svømmede rundt om den og samlede de flydende årer op, surrede dem på tværs over rælingen og kravlede tilbage på vores pladser. Der sad vi, med vand til knæene, med vand over hvert eneste spant og hver eneste planke, så båden, som hang der i vandet, for vore øjne, når vi kiggede ned, lignede en koralbåd, der var vokset op til os fra havbunden.

Vinden steg til et hyl. Bølgerne slog deres skjolde sammen, og hele bygen brølede, forgrenede sig og knitrede rundt om os som en hvid ild på prærien, hvori vi brændte uden at fortæres — udødelige i dødens gab! Forgæves anråbte vi de andre både. Man kunne lige så godt råbe til de glødende kul nede i skorstenen på en rasende ovn som at anråbe de både i den storm. Imens blev den jagende sprøjt, de flyvende skyer og tågen mørkere af nattens skygger. Ingen tegn på skibet var at se. Den stigende sø udelukkede ethvert forsøg på at øse båden læns. Årerne var ubrugelige til roning og tjente nu som redningsbælter. Så skar Starbuck surringen over på den vandtætte tændstikdunk, og efter mange fejlslagne forsøg fik han tændt lampen i lygten. Han satte den fast på en flagstang (stangen med flag, som bruges til at mærke en dræbt hval) og rakte den til Queequeg som fanebærer for dette fortabte håb. Dér sad han så og holdt det svage lys højt midt i den almægtige forladthed. Dér sad han så, tegnet og symbolet på en mand uden tro, der håbløst holder håbet højt midt i fortvivlelsen.

Våde og gennemblødte, rystende af kulde og uden håb om hverken skib eller båd løftede vi øjnene, da dagen gryede. Tågen lå stadig udbredt over havet, og den tomme lygte lå knust i bunden af båden. Pludselig sprang Queequeg op og holdt hånden op til øret. Vi hørte alle en svag knagen, som lyden af tov og rær, som stormen indtil nu havde dæmpet. Den kom nærmere og nærmere. En kæmpemæssig, utydelig skikkelse delte svagt den tykke tåge. I rædsel sprang vi alle i havet, da skibet endelig tonede frem og stod lige ned mod os, knapt mere end sin egen længde fra os.

Fra stedet, hvor vi flød i bølgerne, så vi den forladte båd vippe og gabe et øjeblik under skibets stævn som en træflis for foden af et vandfald. Så rullede det enorme skrog hen over den, og den forsvandt, indtil den dukkede op igen, tumlende, agterude. Vi svømmede efter den igen, blev kastet mod den af søerne og blev til sidst taget op og bragt sikkert om bord. De andre både havde skåret sig løs fra deres fisk, før bygen nåede dem, og var kommet tilbage til skibet i god tid. Skibet havde opgivet os som tabt, men krydsede stadig rundt, hvis det skulle støde på et eller andet tegn på vores død — en åre eller et lanceskaft.
